paper_title: Intercostal Artery Laceration: Rare Complication of Thoracentesis and Role of Ultrasound in Early Detection
disease_label_per_paper: Massive post-thoracentesis hemothorax from posterior intercostal artery laceration
rankable_evidence_window: Use pre-procedure risk context, right thoracentesis exposure, abrupt post-procedure dyspnea and hypoxemia, ultrasound showing recurrent complex right pleural fluid with debris, 2 L bloody pleural drainage, and hemoglobin drop. Do not use thoracotomy source control, postoperative course, myocardial infarction, or death as rankable evidence.

past_history: coronary artery disease after coronary artery bypass graft
end stage renal disease on hemodialysis

presentation_summary: A 63-year-old man with ESRD on hemodialysis, prior CABG, oxygen-dependent COPD, and aspirin use was admitted with dyspnea and bilateral pleural effusions.
On hospital day 2 he required mechanical ventilation for respiratory distress and underwent right diagnostic/therapeutic thoracentesis.
The thoracentesis removed 1100 mL yellow transudative fluid; immediate radiograph showed reduced right effusion and oxygenation improved.
About 8 hours later he developed shortness of breath, blood pressure 100/65 mmHg, heart rate 100/min, and oxygen saturation 88% on 3 L/min nasal oxygen.

Bedside ultrasound showed recurrent large right complex pleural fluid with septations/debris, pigtail catheter drained 2 L bloody fluid, hemoglobin dropped to 7.4 g/dL from about 9 g/dL, and thoracotomy found a bleeding posterior intercostal artery.
source_text_summary: PMC case report of massive hemothorax after right thoracentesis: early post-procedure recurrence of complex right pleural fluid on ultrasound, 2 L bloody drainage, acute hemoglobin decline, transfusion, and thoracotomy with posterior intercostal artery bleeding.

timeline.event: The patient presented with two weeks of dyspnea, bilateral pleural effusions, ESRD on hemodialysis, oxygen-dependent COPD, prior CABG, and aspirin exposure.
Worsening respiratory distress and hypoxemia required mechanical ventilation; bedside ultrasound showed large bilateral anechoic effusions.
Right thoracentesis via an 8 Fr catheter removed 1100 mL yellow transudative fluid with very low RBC count.
About 8 hours later dyspnea and hypoxemia recurred; ultrasound showed large recurrent complex right pleural fluid, pigtail catheter drained 2 L bloody fluid, and hemoglobin dropped.
Right thoracotomy revealed a bleeding posterior intercostal artery at the 8th intercostal space, which was cauterized and clipped.
